tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Using a while loop, display every number from it down to 1, one on each line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
tasks.starter: # Count down to 1 with a while loop

tests.why: Counting down means the number gets smaller every turn. Numbers going up means 1 was added where it should have been taken away.
A 1 gives exactly one turn. Nothing at all means the condition was n > 1 where n >= 1 was needed.
If this one never finished, the variable in the condition was never changed inside the loop, so the condition stays true for ever.

tasks.fb: A while loop tests its condition before every turn, and the variable in that condition must change inside the loop or it runs for ever.

teach.say: A while loop keeps going while its condition is true. The variable the condition uses has to change inside the loop, or the loop never ends.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Using a while loop, display every number from it down to 1, one on each line. Then display go on the last line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which may be 0.
Print exactly: go
tasks.starter: # Count down to 1, then print the last line

tests.why: Three numbers, then the fixed line. A fourth number means the loop went one turn too far.
One turn, then go. Printing go first means that line is above the loop instead of after it.
With 0 the condition is false straight away, so the body never runs. A 0 printed here means a loop that always runs at least once.

tasks.fb: A while loop can run zero times, because its condition is tested before the first turn rather than after it.

teach.say: A line written after the loop is not indented, so it runs once, when the loop has finished.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Then ask for a second whole number, which is never smaller than the first. Using a while loop, display every number from the first to the second, both included, one on each line.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
tasks.starter: # Count up from the first number to the second

tests.why: Both ends are included, so the condition stops after the second number rather than before it.
Two numbers the same give exactly one line. Nothing at all means the condition stopped before the first value was printed.
The count starts at the first number typed. A list beginning at 0 or 1 means that number was ignored.
Four lines. Three means the condition used < where <= was needed, so the last number was left out.

tasks.fb: A counting while loop needs all three parts: set the variable before the loop, test it in the condition, change it inside the loop.

teach.say: A while loop can count upwards too: set the variable to the first value, test it against the last one, and add 1 at the bottom of the loop.

tasks.q: Keep asking the user for a whole number until one of them is 10 or more. Display too small for each number refused. Then display [the accepted number] on a line of its own.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until one of them is 10 or more.
Print exactly: too small
tasks.starter: # Keep asking until the number is 10 or more

tests.why: One number refused, so one warning, then the accepted number on its own line.
The first number is already 10 or more, so nothing is refused. A warning here means the loop body ran before the condition was tested.
Two numbers refused means two warnings. One only means an if was used where a while was needed, because an if checks once and then gives up.
Exactly 10 is accepted. Refusing it means the condition was n <= 10 where n < 10 was needed.

tasks.fb: Read once before the loop, then while the value is still wrong, warn and read again - which is what lets the loop run zero times.

teach.say: Read once before the loop. Then, while the value is still wrong, warn and read again.

tasks.q: Keep asking the user for a whole number until one of them is from 1 to 20. Display out of range for each number refused. Then display [the accepted number] on a line of its own.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until one of them is from 1 to 20.
Print exactly: out of range
tasks.starter: # Keep asking until the number is from 1 to 20

tests.why: Two numbers refused, one below the range and one above it, so both ends of the condition are being tested.
The first number is inside the range, so nothing is printed about it. A warning here means the loop body ran before the condition was tested.
20 is inside the range. Refusing it means the condition used n > 19 or n >= 20 where n > 20 was needed.
21 is just outside and 1 is the bottom of the range, so this is where < and <= get mixed up.

tasks.fb: Two ways of being wrong are joined with or, and the loop keeps going while either of them is still true.

teach.say: Two ways of being wrong are joined with or, because either one of them means asking again.

tasks.q: Keep asking the user for a word until it is yes or no. Display please answer yes or no for each other word. Then display [the accepted word] on a line of its own.
brief: The user types in words, one on each line, until one of them is yes or no.
Print exactly: please answer yes or no
tasks.starter: # Keep asking until the answer is yes or no

tests.why: One word refused, so one warning, then the accepted word on its own line.
no is already one of the two answers, so the loop must not run at all. A warning here means the body ran before the condition was tested.
Two words refused means two warnings, and both yes and no are accepted. If only one of them works, the condition tests for a single word.
y is not the word yes, so it is refused. Comparing only the first letter accepts words the question rules out.

tasks.fb: Two words are allowed, so the condition rules out both with and: not yes or not no is always true and loops for ever.

teach.say: Two answers are allowed, so the loop has to keep going while the word is neither of them - which means and, not or.
code: c = input("Colour? ")   # the user types pink

tasks.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type -1, which is the signal to stop. Display each number as it is typed, one on each line. Do not display the -1.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
At least one number comes before the -1.
tasks.starter: # Print each number until -1 stops the loop

tests.why: Three numbers, three lines. A -1 on the end means it was printed before the condition was tested again.
One number before the signal gives one line.
A 0 is ordinary data here and is printed like any other number, because only -1 stops the loop.

tasks.fb: A sentinel is a value that cannot be real data and means stop: read one before the loop, use it inside, then read the next at the bottom of the body.

teach.say: Read one value before the loop. Use it inside the loop, then read the next one at the bottom of the body, so the condition is tested again before that value is used.

tasks.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type -1, which is the signal to stop and is not added. Add the numbers up. Display [the total] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
With no numbers at all the total is 0.
tasks.starter: # Add the numbers up until -1 stops the loop

tests.why: The three numbers come to 250. A 249 means the -1 was added as well, and the signal is not data.
No numbers at all, so the total is still 0. A crash means a number was read after the -1.
One number only. Check the total starts at 0 before the loop rather than at the first number.
However many numbers there are, the same loop handles them, so a program written for a fixed count fails here.

tasks.fb: A running total in a while loop is the same three steps as in a for loop: set it before, add inside, print after.

teach.say: The total is set to 0 before the loop, added to inside it, and printed once the loop has finished.

tasks.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type the word end, which is the signal to stop. Add the numbers up. Display [the total] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, then the word end to finish.
With no numbers at all the total is 0.
tasks.starter: # Add the numbers up until the word end stops the loop

tests.why: The three numbers come to 54. Each line has to be cast with int() before it can be added.
The loop runs zero times. A crash means int() was used on the word end - read the line as text first and convert it only once the condition has let it through.
One number only, and the total still has to be printed.
Negative numbers lower the total. int() copes with the minus sign, but the line still has to be read as text first.

tasks.fb: When the sentinel is a word, the line is read as text and cast to a number only once the condition has let it through.

teach.say: A sentinel can be a word, so read the line as text and only turn it into a number once you know it is not the sentinel.

tasks.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type -1. Count how many numbers were typed. Display [the count] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
The -1 is not counted.
tasks.starter: # Count the numbers until -1 stops the loop

tests.why: Four numbers were typed. A 5 means the -1 was counted as one of them.
Nothing was typed, so the count is 0, and that 0 still has to be printed.
One number gives a count of 1.
A 0 is a number like any other and still counts, because only -1 stops the loop.

tasks.fb: A counter goes up by 1 on every turn, which counts the turns however large or small the values are.

teach.say: A counter is a total that goes up by 1, so it is set to 0 before the loop and raised once on every turn.

tasks.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type -1. Count how many of them are 40 or more. Display [the count] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
Exactly 40 counts as 40 or more.
tasks.starter: # Count only the numbers that reach 40

tests.why: Two of the four reach 40, and only the count is printed.
No numbers at all, so the count is 0. The counter has to be set before the loop so it still has a value when the loop runs zero times.
39 does not reach 40. A 1 here means >= 39 was used where >= 40 was needed.
Exactly 40 counts, so all three do. A 1 here means > 40 was used instead of >= 40.

tasks.fb: The if inside the loop is what makes a counter count some turns and ignore the rest.

teach.say: An if inside the loop decides which turns count, so the counter goes up on some turns and not on others.

tasks.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type -1. Count how many numbers were typed, not counting the -1. Count how many of them are 40 or more. Display [how many were typed]. Then display [how many reach 40] on the next line.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
Two lines of output: how many were typed, then how many reach 40.
Exactly 40 counts as 40 or more.
tasks.starter: # Count the numbers, and count how many reach 40

tests.why: Four numbers, two of which reach 40. A 5 on the first line means the -1 was counted.
No numbers at all, so both counts are 0 and both lines still print.
One number, which does not reach 40, so the two lines differ.
Every number reaches 40, so the two lines match - but they are still two separate counters.

tasks.fb: Two counters, both set to 0 before the loop: one counts every turn, the other only the turns where the if is true.

teach.say: Each thing you are tracking needs its own variable, set up before the loop and changed only where it should be.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Start a value at 1 in your program. Keep doubling that value until it is equal to or greater than the number typed in. Count how many doublings that took. Display [how many doublings were needed] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
The value starts at 1, fixed in your program, and is not typed in.
tasks.starter: # Double until the number is reached, counting the doublings

tests.why: 1 doubles to 2, then 4, then 8, which is three doublings. A 4 means the loop went round once more after the value had been reached.
The value starts at 1, which already reaches the target, so no doubling is needed. A 1 here means a loop that always runs once.
After two doublings the value is 4, which is not yet 5, so a third is needed: the loop stops once the number is reached or passed, not only on an exact match.
The values go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. A program written for small numbers is wrong here.

tasks.fb: A condition-controlled loop is for when the number of turns depends on what happens, which is why while and not for is the right choice here.

teach.say: When you cannot know how many turns are needed before you start, a while loop is the right choice and a for loop is not. Count the turns in a variable of your own.

tasks.q: Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers, using a for loop. Work out the largest of them. Display [the largest] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow, which is never less than 1.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
The numbers may be negative.
tasks.starter: # Read the numbers with a for loop, keeping the largest

tests.why: Four numbers, and the largest is not the last one, so the best so far has to be remembered rather than printed at the end of the loop.
With one number, that number is the largest.
Every number is below 0, so a best so far that started at 0 could never be beaten. Start it at the first number instead.
All four are the same, so the first one is already the largest and nothing replaces it.

tasks.fb: The count is known before the loop starts, so a for loop fits, and the best so far has to start at the first value rather than at 0.

teach.say: When the count is known before the loop starts, a for loop is the right choice. A best so far starts at the first value, because a guess of 0 could never be beaten by a negative one.

tasks.q: Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers, using a for loop. Work out the largest of them. Then, using a while loop, keep asking for one more number at a time until one of them is equal to or greater than that largest number. Display too small for each number refused. Then display ok on a line of its own.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow, which may be 0.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line, none of them below 0.
With no numbers at all the first number tested is accepted.
Print exactly: too small, and then ok
tasks.starter: # A for loop for the numbers, a while loop for the one being tested

tests.why: The largest number read is 25, so 20 and 24 are both refused before 25 is accepted. One warning only means an if was used where a while was needed.
30 is above the largest number read, so the while loop runs zero times. A warning here means the comparison used the last number read rather than the largest.
With 0 numbers the for loop runs zero times, so nothing is read and the first number tested is accepted. A crash means a number was read anyway.
A number equal to the largest is accepted, so the condition is < and not <=.
Two equal numbers, then one refused. Reading more than one number per turn of the while loop puts the lines out of step.

tasks.fb: Use for when the number of turns is known before you start and while when it depends on what the user does next - this question needs one of each.

teach.say: One program can use both kinds of loop: for while the count is known, while for the part that depends on what the user types next.
code: answer = input("Done? ")   # the user types n

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number that is 0 or more. Add up its digits without turning the number into text. Display [the total of the digits] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in one whole number that is 0 or more.
Take the digits off with arithmetic rather than turning the number into text.
tasks.starter: # Take the last digit off the number on every turn

tests.why: 4 + 7 + 2 is 13. A 2 means the loop went round once only - the number has to be divided down inside the loop as well as having its last digit taken.
0 has no digits to take off, so the loop runs zero times and the total is still 0. No output at all means the total was never set before the loop.
A single digit. A 0 here means the condition stopped the loop before the last digit was used.
Only the 1 counts, because the zeros add nothing. If this never finished, / was used instead of //, so the number never reaches 0 exactly.
Five nines make 45. A program that only looked at two or three digits comes up short here.

tasks.fb: n % 10 gives the last digit and n // 10 removes it, and // is what lets the number reach 0 so the loop can stop.

teach.say: n % 10 gives the last digit and n // 10 takes it off. // keeps the answer whole, so the number reaches 0 exactly.

tasks.q: The whole number 37 is fixed in your program. Keep asking the user for a whole number until they type 37. Display higher when the number typed is below 37. Display lower when it is above 37. Display correct when it is 37.
brief: The 37 is fixed in your program and not typed in.
One line of output for every number typed.
Print exactly: higher, lower and correct
tasks.starter: # The fixed number is 37. Say which way to go.

tests.why: 10 is below 37 so the answer is higher, and 50 is above it so the answer is lower. Swapping these two means the message says what the number was rather than which way to go.
The first number is already 37, so no other line is printed. A hint here means the loop body ran before the condition was tested.
Two numbers above 37. If this never finished, the message was printed but no new number was read inside the loop.
36 is one below, so the answer is higher. Comparing with <= 37 would print a message for 37 itself as well.

tasks.fb: The condition decides whether to keep going and the if inside the loop decides what to say, and the new value must be read inside the loop or nothing ever changes.

teach.say: The condition tests only whether the value is the one wanted. An if inside the loop chooses which of the two messages to print.

tasks.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type the word end. Count how many numbers were typed. Add them up. Work out the largest of them. Display [how many were typed]. Then display [the total] on the next line. Then display [the largest] on the next line. Display none on a line of its own instead when end is the very first line.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, then the word end to finish.
The numbers may be negative.
Print exactly: none
tasks.starter: # Count them, total them, and remember the largest

tests.why: Three numbers coming to 95, the largest being 45. A 20 on the last line means the final number was printed rather than the largest.
The loop runs zero times, so there is nothing to report. Three zeros mean the empty case was never checked, and a crash means the word end was converted to a number.
With one number the total and the largest are both that number.
All three are below 0, so a largest that started at 0 could never be beaten. Start it at the first number read.
The largest is in the middle, so a program that only looked at the first or the last number is wrong here.

tasks.fb: A count, a total and a best so far can all be kept in one pass, and all three must be set up before the loop so the empty case still works.

teach.say: One pass can keep a count, a running total and a best so far at the same time, as long as each has its own variable set up before the loop.

tasks.q: Which kind of loop does each job need?
items: Ask until a valid locker number is typed
Keep guessing until the number is right
Add up a known number of marks
Double the weed until it covers the pond
tasks.fb: If you can say the number of repeats before the loop starts, use for.

info.title: Stuck forever
info.text: If a program stops responding, an infinite loop is often why: the condition it waits for can never become False.

info.title: Ask again politely
info.text: A good validation loop says what was wrong with the last answer, not just 'try again'.

info.title: Choosing a sentinel
info.text: -1 works when the real values can never be negative. For a temperature it would be a terrible choice.

info.title: Count or total
info.text: A counter always adds 1. A running total adds whatever came in. Plenty of programs need both at once.

info.title: Testing at the bottom
info.text: Some languages have a loop that tests its condition at the end, so it always runs once. Python does not, so the first read goes above the loop.

info.title: No data at all
info.text: A program given no data should still print something sensible. Start every total at zero and it will.
